source.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Zheng-Fu He; Wentao Shu; Xuyang Ge; Lingjie Chen; Junxuan Wang; Yunhua Zhou; Frances Liu; Qi-Peng Guo; Xuan-Jing Huang; Zu-Xuan Wu; Yu-Gang Jiang; Xi-Peng Qiu

page_placements.theme: Semantic neighborhoods, feature families and hierarchy

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies and evaluates SAEs on Llama-3.1-8B, reporting interpretability and feature-geometry results relevant to whether sparse features can be recovered in an LLM. It does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper states the superposition hypothesis as background, but that description and cited findings are not results from this study. Its SAE sparsity and reconstruction evaluations assess the trained dictionaries, not whether the underlying model would represent features differently without the SAE sparsity constraint. The paper's prompt for GPT-4o to score feature interpretations is an evaluation prompt, not an instruction addressed to an AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: This is mainly an SAE resource paper, but its interpretability scoring of randomly sampled features bears on V4 (recoverable sparse features in Llama-3.1-8B). Its TopK-vs-Vanilla decoder matching and 8x-vs-32x comparison bear on V5 (stability or canonicality of dictionary features). It does not reproduce toy models.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors release 256 TopK SAEs for Llama-3.1-8B and report that TopK beats Vanilla on the sparsity-fidelity trade-off, with similar interpretability. They report that the SAEs generalize to long contexts and instruct models, that TopK and Vanilla share feature geometry, and that wider SAEs learn new features. The last two claims rest on figure-level and anecdotal evidence.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates SAEs on Llama-3.1-8B; it does not run the original toy-network feature-sparsity and geometric-transition experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE width changes the reported feature inventory; longer contexts modestly worsen reconstruction loss and L0 sparsity; SAE results differ at the near-output L31R positions on instruction-finetuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected neighbouring SAE features form a semantically coherent cluster. Their farthest pairwise cosine is 0.28, against a random-projection maximum of 0.09–0.10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE decoder directions form semantic neighbourhoods in the residual stream.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on the base model transfer to longer contexts with mild degradation (12% higher MSE, L0 rising from 50 to 55). They also transfer to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, except at L31R.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Base-model SAEs generalize across context length and to instruction fine-tuning.

record.problems: Interpretability analysis uses a small random subset of 768 features from three layers and relies on GPT-4o scoring; manual analysis covers only a subset. The authors note that focusing on top activations may miss low-activation behavior. The feature-geometry case study selects a single feature cluster, and cosine similarity is not a direct measure of semantic similarity. Several numerical distributions are shown only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted for the 60-row limit. Background statements about superposition and cited results from other work were excluded.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity sweep and no geometry transition.
Neuron polysemanticity and capacity competition are not studied.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity are not studied.
No comparison of SAE features with neurons. The claim of spreading across neurons is not tested.
Completeness is not directly tested; only explained variance is reported. Canonicality is not tested beyond one width example.
Multi-dimensional versus one-dimensional features are not tested.

missing.what: Sparsity-fidelity results: explained variance of about 0.65–0.76 and Delta LM loss at L0≈50 for L7R, L15R and L23R residual SAEs. TopK beats Vanilla (L0 about 150 to 50), and wider SAEs reconstruct better. This is relevant to completeness under V5.
Firing-frequency results: training targets about 10% inactive features and fewer than 2% ultra-active features. Wider SAEs shift toward lower firing frequency.
Figure 8 includes an L15R-32x TopK-vs-Vanilla similarity curve that is not recorded.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a tool or resource paper; its evidence on the claim is indirect. Only a few rows bear on versions, and the generalization rows concern the tool's own performance. The GPT-4o prompt in the appendix is evaluation material and was not followed.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks or feature-sparsity/importance sweep testing superposition geometry or its transition.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as a consequence of limited representational capacity or feature importance.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

The study does not establish that features are spread across many neurons, or compare SAE recovery with neuron-based representations. It evaluates selected SAE features and their generalization, rather than exhaustively validating the recovered features as the model's features.
It compares decoder-feature geometry across TopK and Vanilla SAEs and reports a width-dependent example, but does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units.
The paper treats decoder columns as directions and measures their cosine similarity, but does not compare one-dimensional features with multi-dimensional features.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Manual interpretability assessment of selected SAE features

conditions.value: subset of the 768 features selected for automated analysis

rows.measure: Fraction of manually assessed features with monosemanticity score 1 (not interpretable)
rows.note: The authors say manual analysis was consistent with automated analysis. This is a selected feature subset, and the manual analysis does not distinguish scores 2–5.
rows.check: The features are a random sample, not a selected one. About 90% were judged interpretable at some level, which is the effect V4 names, so the state should be observed rather than partial. The manual subset size is not stated.

source_check.problem: The stored subset description is correct. The accompanying verdict fix overstates random sampling: the automated sample was random, but selection of the manually assessed subset is unspecified.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: GPT-4o automated monosemanticity scoring from the 20 most activating contexts per feature

conditions.value: 128 randomly selected features from each of L7R-8x, L15R-8x, and L23R-8x for each variant; 768 total

rows.value: figure only; authors report no significant difference between TopK and Vanilla SAEs
rows.note: The text reports no significant difference between variants, but does not give numerical score proportions. The study notes that evaluation of top activations may miss behavior on low-activating samples.
rows.check: The condition is inconsistent. Figure 3 shows only L15R-8x, while the sample covers L7R, L15R and L23R. Score proportions appear only in the figure.

source_check.correct: Separate the three-layer automated evaluation protocol from the displayed distribution: 128 features per layer and variant, 768 total; Figure 3 specifically names L15R-8x. Its readable distribution shows predominantly interpretable features, supporting state=observed for V4. The source does not resolve whether the chart pools layers.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3 and Figure 3, p. 9; required image page-09.png.
source_check.problem: The condition combines a single-layer chart with the full three-layer sample; this originates in a source-internal caption/narrative ambiguity. With the image available, cannot_determine no longer describes the V4 result.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Measured decoder-column cosine similarity among selected features in a threats-to-humanity case study

conditions.value: 36 selected features from L15R-8x-Vanilla, L15R-8x-TopK, and L15R-32x-TopK

rows.measure: Farthest pairwise cosine similarity among the 36 selected features
rows.baseline: random-projection maximum pairwise cosine similarity: 0.09 for 8x and 0.10 for 32x
rows.locator: Section 4.6, “How Close Enough are Features to Be Neighbors?”
rows.note: The authors say the selected features have non-trivial similarity and describe a coherent theme across them, including wars, pandemics, disasters, and other harmful events. Cosine similarity is explicitly not treated as a direct measure of semantic similarity.
rows.check: This is a hand-picked cluster of 36 features chosen as nearest neighbours of one seed. Its cosine similarity versus a random baseline shows semantic neighbourhoods, not recovery, stability or canonicality of features.

source_check.problem: The source uses the imprecise term cosine similarity distance for 0.28. The selected neighborhood and random comparison are correctly recorded; this does not directly test a claim version.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Randomly mapped features into a 4096-dimensional space to estimate maximum pairwise cosine similarity
rows.locator: Section 4.6, “How Close Enough are Features to Be Neighbors?”
rows.note: Randomly mapped features are the comparison baseline for the selected-feature geometry result.
rows.check: This is a random-projection baseline for R3, not a result on any version.

source_check.correct: Subject: synthetic randomly mapped feature vectors in D=4096 dimensions, with F=8×4096 or 32×4096; no Llama checkpoint is evaluated in this control.
source_check.problem: The numerical control concerns synthetic vectors rather than measurements from Llama-3.1-8B-Base.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Compared each L15R-8x-TopK feature's decoder column with its most similar L15R-8x-Vanilla counterpart
rows.measure: Cumulative distribution of maximum pairwise cosine similarities between features
rows.baseline: random baseline: maximum cosine similarity between two random SAEs of the same size
rows.value: figure only; the authors state similarities are significantly higher than the random baseline
rows.locator: Figure 8 and Section 4.6, “TopK SAEs Learn Similar Features to Vanilla SAEs”
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that TopK and Vanilla SAEs share a universal feature geometry; the numerical distribution is not stated in the text.
rows.check: This is a stability-across-architecture result, so it bears on V5 and not V4. Figure 8 also plots an L15R-32x curve, which the row omits. Values are given only in the figure.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.6 and Figure 8, p. 13; required image page-13.png.
source_check.problem: The text supports the same-width 8x comparison and states superiority to random controls. Figure 8 additionally contains a 32x curve but does not display the random baseline; omitting the additional curve does not invalidate this condition-specific row.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Compared features from wider and narrower SAEs in a decoder-feature geometry case study
rows.measure: Presence of a distinct feature for Brexit in the wider SAE compared with the most similar feature in smaller SAEs
rows.baseline: The most similar features in the smaller SAEs are described as a more general Historical Movements feature
rows.value: A distinct Brexit feature in L15R-32x-TopK, described as activating exclusively on this topic
rows.locator: Section 4.6, “Wider SAEs Do Learn New Features”
rows.note: The authors say the wider feature is not merely a linear combination of features from the smaller SAE.
rows.check: This is a single anecdotal example, and it shows feature splitting with width. It bears on canonicality (V5), not V4. As evidence against canonical units it supports limits_scope.

source_check.correct: state=partial for V5: the width-dependent Brexit versus Historical Movements example qualifies canonicality of the feature inventory. The feature-splitting observation itself is reported.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.6, p. 13, Wider SAEs Do Learn New Features; Figure 7, p. 12.
source_check.problem: Observed describes the feature-splitting finding, whereas the linked V5 claim requires stable, canonical units; the anecdote instead qualifies that claim.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE reconstruction loss and sparsity on longer-context data

conditions.value: 166 L-Eval documents, truncated to 8192 tokens; 1.3 million tokens

rows.measure: Average reconstruction loss in the last 1024 tokens and L0 sparsity
rows.baseline: Training data: L0 sparsity 50; reconstruction-loss comparison is reported as an increase from training data
rows.value: Last 1024 tokens: reconstruction loss 0.0086, a 12% increase compared to training data; L0 sparsity increases from 50 to 55
rows.note: The paper reports these as results for Llama Scope SAEs on long-context data; the stated average is not broken out by width in the text.
rows.check: This is out-of-distribution performance of the authors' SAEs on long contexts, i.e. the tool's own generalization, not a measure of whether the model contains such features.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.5.1 and Figure 5, p. 10; required image page-10.png.
source_check.problem: The prose gives 0.0086, 12%, and L0 50→55 without a width-specific attribution. Figure 5 shows distinct 8x and 32x curves, so these prose summaries should not be treated as identical measurements for both widths.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Applied SAEs trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Base to activations from instruction-finetuned models and measured L0 sparsity and Delta LM loss

conditions.value: subset of Wildchat with 4K chat histories

rows.measure: Change in Delta LM loss and L0 sparsity relative to the reported base-model SAE evaluation
rows.baseline: Base-model evaluation; no single aggregate value stated
rows.value: No significant degradation in Delta LM loss or increase in L0 sparsity across SAEs other than L31R-8x and L31R-32x
rows.note: The result is stated for the set of SAEs as an aggregate; the near-output exceptions are not explored further.
rows.check: This measures SAE transfer to the instruct model, which is the tool's performance. The L31R exceptions are not explored.

source_check.problem: The narrative supports the stored all-layer, two-width evaluation and L31R exceptions. Figure 6's caption incorrectly names only L15R-8x despite plotting layers and both widths; this is a source-internal disagreement.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Replaced L15R activations with their SAE reconstructions and measured language-model loss
rows.baseline: 0.162 for the corresponding replacement in the base model
rows.value: 0.090 for the instruction-finetuned model; same L0 sparsity as the base-model evaluation
rows.note: The authors caution that the smaller Delta LM loss does not necessarily mean the SAE is better suited to the instruct model; downstream tasks may be more robust to perturbations.
rows.check: This measures SAE transfer performance. The authors say the lower Delta LM loss reflects task robustness to perturbation, not a better fit.

relationships.reason: Max decoder cosine similarities between architectures are well above the random-SAE baseline; the authors call it a shared geometry (R5, figure only).

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: L15R TopK versus Vanilla SAEs of the same width
source_check.reason: R5 supports correspondence across SAE architectures in the tested same-width 8x setting. The above-random result is stated explicitly in Section 4.6; it supports the stability aspect without establishing completeness or full canonicality.

relationships.reason: The 32x SAE has a distinct Brexit feature, while the smaller SAEs have only a general Historical Movements feature, so the feature inventory depends on width (R6).

source_check.condition: L15R TopK SAEs at 8x versus 32x width
source_check.reason: R6 reports a distinct Brexit feature at 32x whose closest smaller-SAE counterparts are broader historical features, qualifying a width-independent canonical inventory. This is a single selected example.

relationships.reason: Based on the text: explained variance is about 0.65–0.76 at L0 around 50, so the dictionaries leave a substantial residual and are incomplete. No row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Explained variance was about 0.65–0.76 at L0 near 50, leaving a substantial residual.

source_check.condition: Residual-stream SAEs at L0≈50 (text/Figure 2, no row)

relation.reason: The study evaluates recovered features and their correspondence across SAE choices, rather than reporting only tool performance.

source_check.notes: The official PDF's title, authors, abstract and arXiv:2410.20526v1 date (27 Oct 2024) match the supplied snapshot; its SHA256 matches the manifest, with no material version difference found. All three required images were inspected and readable, with none missing or failed; remaining caption/narrative inconsistencies are source-internal, not extraction failures or version mismatches.

statements.correction: Llama-3.1-8B-Base; TopK and Vanilla 8x SAEs at L7R/L15R/L23R; automated sample=768 randomly selected features; manual assessment=unspecified subset; about 10% uninterpretable; no neuron comparison.
statements.problem: About 10% is correctly reported, but the manual subset is not explicitly described as randomly selected. Random selection is established for the parent automated sample.

The qualitative above-random comparison is stated in the prose; Figure 8 supplies distributions without a plotted random control. This is evidence of correspondence, with completeness and full canonicality untested by this comparison.
